newsitem.title: FRANCE: French teachers strike in job cuts protest.
newsitem.headline: French teachers strike in job cuts protest.

text.p: French teachers stayed away from school on Monday, forcing hundreds to close and disrupting others in a one-day strike over government plans to shed several thousand jobs including short-term helpers.

Teaching unions, in a litmus test for likely labour unrest in coming weeks, claimed victory a few hours into the school day with an estimate that more than 80 percent of primary school teachers heeded their strike call.
In Paris, organisers said 20,000 people took part in a march through the students' Latin Quarter to the Education Ministry. Police said the number was closer to 10,000.
Chanting "Education mustn't go bust", thousands more protested in some 60 other cities and towns.
The stoppage was the first in four years called jointly by the country's five biggest teachers' unions, which represent some 825,000 teachers. They advised parents to keep their children at home.
The Syndicat des Enseignants union said the strike rallied 70 percent of teachers in junior high schools and nearly 60 percent in high schools.
A spokeswoman for the Education Ministry put the number of strikers at 59 percent in the primary sector, 44 percent in secondary schools and 20 percent among administrative personnel.
Several hundred schools were forced to close, she said.
The government has announced plans to eliminate more than 5,000 jobs in primary and secondary education in 1997 as a result of falling birthrates in recent years.
Some 2,700 new posts will be created in higher education but teachers say that will still mean 2,300 fewer jobs in total.
Unions also say that close to 15,000 of the 28,000 short-term teachers hired for the last school year had not had their contracts renewed and had thus lost their jobs.
The government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe is under fire for its budget and economic policies after unemployment reached a record 12.6 percent last month.
Unions have been predicting significant unrest in coming months and a big civil service strike is set for October 17.
Marc Blondel, leader of Force Ouvriere, one of France's three biggest unions, accused Juppe of failing to stay in touch with unions.
"Since October of last year, Juppe's labour affairs adviser hasn't called me once. When you lead a country you have to be in touch with those who represent part of that country," he said.
Opinion polls show Juppe's popularity ratings at near-record lows, and some deputies in the governing centre-right are openly pleading for change well ahead of 1998 general elections.
But so far there has been little evidence of dissatisfaction of the magnitude that led to last year's crippling public sector strikes in a four-week period during November and December.
In a separate protest, train drivers at state-owned SNCF struck on Monday in a protest at working hours in the eastern suburbs of Paris, cutting services by a third.
